schools.summary: Gregory the Great explains why a man who is losing an argument repeats what everyone knows, and distinguishes wisdom held by participation from wisdom held by comparison with God.
Gill has Eliphaz leading every round of the dispute and betaking himself to calumny instead of solid reasons, and calls the doctrine a great truth misapplied.
Henry grounds the denial in the question of debt and holds the innuendo drawn from Job's complaints to be a strained one.
Clarke turns the principle on the sufferer, that God has no interest in his conduct; Wesley reduces the charge to Job insisting on his own righteousness as if he obliged God by it.

Ellicott hears a far more exaggerated and offensive tone and makes the judgment of God necessarily disinterested; Keil and Delitzsch trace the verb for being profitable, which belongs to this book alone.

debates.question: Can the commonplace Eliphaz states be charged against Job?

sides.position: Very true and good in itself, but unjustly applied, since Job was far from thinking God unjust
Job's insistence on his own righteousness amounts to obliging God by it

debates.question: Is the clause about the wise man part of the question or a statement of its own?

sides.position: Probably an independent statement
A truth in its own right, that our wisdom and piety are what we gain by

outliers.note: He alone accounts for the repetition of a commonplace: those who get the worst in making out a case often repeat what is well known, lest by holding their tongue they should seem defeated.

themes: can a man be profitable unto God
the wise man profitable to himself
the tone of the third round
1.pericope_label: Eliphaz answers: can a man be profitable unto God?

schools.summary: Gill grants at length that God takes pleasure in his people as righteous in Christ, then denies that any of it adds to the complacency of his mind.
Henry supplies the political figure of curbing a subject's greatness, the slander told to our first parents, and the instances of Pharaoh and Herod.
Clarke rests the case on the divine perfections, which neither gain nor lose by men; Wesley narrows the pleasure to what God would need for his own ease and contentment.
Ellicott sharpens the second question into God standing in awe of Job and justifying his dealings with him.

debates.question: What does the phrase rendered "for fear of thee" mean?

sides.position: Out of fear of Job, as magistrates punish offenders who might overturn the state
For thy fear of God, thy piety, or as Broughton has it, for thy religion
Because he standeth in awe of thee

outliers.note: He alone supplies the history, Pharaoh oppressing Israel because he feared them and Herod slaying the children of Bethlehem, to show what punishing out of fear looks like in men.

themes: no new pleasure added to God
for thy fear or for thy piety
the oldest form of the slander
3.pericope_label: Is it any pleasure to the Almighty that thou art righteous?

schools.summary: Gill concedes that all wickedness is great as committed against God, and that sensible sinners own it most readily, which singles nobody out.
Henry marks this as the point where the accusation descends to particulars, and turns the occasion into two lessons, anger at unjust censure and pity for the censured.
Clarke reads the second clause as duration rather than number; Wesley compresses the whole argument into a proportion between calamity and sin.
Ellicott refuses the premise as mere conjecture from a false assumption about whom a just God may punish.

debates.question: What is meant by calling the iniquities infinite?

sides.position: More than could be counted and more heinous than could be conceived, since sin against Infinite Majesty has a kind of infinite malignity
Duration rather than number: there is no end to his continuance in them

outliers.note: He alone attacks the reasoning rather than the charge, calling it conjecture arising from the false assumption that a just God can punish only the wicked.

themes: infinite in number or in duration
innocency no shield against a foul tongue
5.pericope_label: Is not thy wickedness great, and thine iniquities infinite?

schools.summary: Gill will not read "for nought" strictly, and records the harsher rendering in which the brothers themselves stand as the pledge.
Henry takes both readings together, adds the stripped clothing the law of Moses forbade, and reads the bread clause as forbidding the giving.
Clarke makes the exaction a settled habit rather than an incident; Wesley has Eliphaz speaking by strong presumption from the unusual calamities.
Ellicott measures the depth to which Eliphaz had sunk by the specificity of charges he could not prove.

debates.question: What was taken as a pledge?

sides.position: A pawn of great value demanded for an inconsiderable debt
The brothers themselves, to be sold or held as bondmen because they had nothing to pay

outliers.note: He alone documents the custom behind the water, including the Indian devotees who stand on the public roads with a skin of water for travellers parched with thirst.

6.pericope_label: Thou hast stripped the naked of their clothing

schools.summary: Gill offers both senses, the mighty man enjoying what Job was too weak to prevent, or holding what Job as judge handed him.
Henry makes it a matter of the courts, takes the harshest version of the widows' dismissal, and presses the passive voice of the last clause.
Clarke glosses the man of arm as the man of influence, rapine and plunder, and ends with the spoils of the defenceless; Wesley reads the possession as held by Job's sentence or permission.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both point the title at Job himself, and Keil and Delitzsch fill out the portrait of a man who fills the place out alone.

sides.position: Job himself
Another man whom Job favoured in his courts

outliers.note: He alone makes the passive voice the point, arguing that connivance in the breaking of the fatherless brings the guilt back on the man in power.

8.pericope_label: The mighty man had the earth, and the widows were sent away empty

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes snares that occasion sin from snares that punish it, and itemises the calamities that beset Job.
Henry states the syllogism behind "therefore", locates the sudden fear in conscience, and warns that those who show no mercy may be denied the hope of finding it.
Clarke makes it a rule of retributive exchange and supplies the hunted elephant; Wesley reads the verse as a choice between fear of further evils and present darkness.
Keil and Delitzsch refuse the incidental construction of the clause and put it as a direct question.

debates.question: How should the clause about darkness be construed?

sides.position: As an incidental clause, whether affirmative or interrogative
holders: the older expositors, as reported by Keil and Delitzsch

sides.position: As a direct question: dost thou not perceive the darkness and the overflow of waters?
The text is damaged, and the word rendered "or" was originally the word for light

outliers.note: He alone suspects the text, canvassing the Septuagint, Houbigant and Good before settling for a plain sense of his own.

themes: snares that punish rather than tempt
10.pericope_label: Snares are round about thee, and darkness that thou canst not see

schools.summary: Gill expounds the height of heaven while insisting God is not confined there, and sets out the atheistical reasoning Job is supposed to hold.
Henry names the manoeuvre of holding the truth in unrighteousness, and answers both forms of the denial, by the transparent firmament and by the reach of the sun.
Clarke protests that the sentiments are fathered on a man who never held them; Wesley makes the height a vantage point and notes that many Heathen philosophers held the opposite.
Keil and Delitzsch trace the charge to the unbelief the Psalms often mention and compare Epicurus on gods who know nothing of earth.

debates.question: Did Job hold what Eliphaz imputes to him?

sides.position: No; these were sentiments Job never held and never uttered
Eliphaz suspected him of them and drew them as an invidious consequence from his complaints

outliers.note: He alone generalises the tactic: dress a man in a bear's skin and he may be hunted and worried by his own dogs, which is how polemic writers in theology and politics often proceed.

themes: God in the height of heaven
12.pericope_label: Is not God in the height of heaven? and how doth God know?

schools.summary: Gill identifies the travellers as the way of Cain and of the old world, and describes the beaten road their life made of sin.
Henry explains why the appeal to history comes here, pairs the Flood with Sodom, and grants the text itself sound however it is being used.
Clarke takes it for another accusation and finds an evident allusion to the Flood; Wesley glosses the phrase as the way of antiquity and its end.
Ellicott re-renders the question to ask not whether Job has observed the old way but whether he keeps it and holds its tenets.

debates.question: Is the question about having marked the old way or about walking in it?

sides.position: Dost thou keep it, and hold the tenets of those who trod it?
Hast thou marked it, and seen what the end of it was?

outliers.note: He alone reads the choice of examples as a reply to Job's argument from the prosperity of the wicked, single instances being set against destructions by wholesale.

themes: the old way wicked men have trodden
a sound text put to a wrong use
15.pericope_label: Hast thou marked the old way which wicked men have trodden?

schools.summary: Gill allows all three senses of being cut down out of time, and supplies the axe at the root and the scythe.
Henry reads the foundation as the ground these men built on, adds the parallel of building upon sand, and gives three construals of the closing question.
Clarke turns the line into reported speech in the mouths of Noah's contemporaries and records a variant that quotes them directly; Wesley notes the words are Job's own, used to a contrary purpose.
Ellicott prefers "snatched away before their time" and draws a consequence about the age of the record of the Flood.

debates.question: What was overflown with a flood?

sides.position: The earth these men built themselves and all their hopes upon
Their foundation became like a flowing stream, their principles being infectious and bearing all before them

outliers.note: He alone turns the allusion to the Flood into an argument about the date of that record, since the book itself can hardly fail to be very old.

themes: depart from us, in Job's own words
what can the Almighty do for them
16.pericope_label: Cut down out of time, they said unto God, Depart from us

schools.summary: Gill makes the bounty temporal and good in itself, and gives three reasons why the righteous may be glad at ruin without delighting in misery.
Henry turns the shared repudiation into a rule for disputants and is careful about the object of the gladness and the manner of the scorn.
Clarke hears sarcasm in the quoted repudiation and reads the gladness as submission to providence; Wesley allows the prosperity but dates its end.
Ellicott makes the irony reach its climax in the borrowed formula; Keil and Delitzsch set the verse beside the close of many Psalms.

debates.question: In what tone does Eliphaz quote Job's own repudiation of the wicked?

sides.position: Sarcastically, having just ranked Job among the impious
Straight, as genuine agreement against those who live without God in the world
With reflection, since Job said it against his own principle

outliers.note: He alone draws from the shared repudiation a rule for disputants, that differences in religion must not weaken unanimity against atheism and irreligion.

themes: the counsel of the wicked far from me
18.pericope_label: Yet he filled their houses with good things

schools.summary: Gill canvasses and rejects two readings before hearing Eliphaz and his friends rank themselves among the innocent.
Henry calls the inference a deceitful rule to judge by, since none knows love or hatred from what is before him, and puts thankfulness in place of censure.
Clarke identifies the remnant as those consumed by fire after the Flood had taken the rest, and names the leverage the two examples are for; Wesley fastens on the change of pronoun.
Ellicott takes the words for the speech of the righteous and renders them accordingly.

debates.question: Whose words are "our substance is not cut down"?

sides.position: The righteous and the innocent of the previous verse
Eliphaz and his friends, ranking themselves among them with an eye on Job's case

outliers.note: He alone says plainly what the two examples are for: to terrify Job into compliance with the exhortation that follows immediately.

themes: whose substance is not cut down
a deceitful rule to judge by
20.pericope_label: Our substance is not cut down, but the remnant of them the fire consumeth

schools.summary: Gill notes the better temper of the advice and what the exhortation presupposes about every man's estrangement from God.
Henry almost forgives the earlier censures for the sake of the counsel, explains the two-sided strategy, and spells out what acquaintance and peace involve.
Clarke proposes that the verb means to treasure up an interest with God, and divides the promised good in two; Wesley lists what renewing the acquaintance takes.
Ellicott offers the alternative that thine increase shall be good, or that what comes is rest from the obstinate questionings Job was disturbed with.

debates.question: What does "acquaint now thyself with him" ask for?

sides.position: Acquiesce in God, quieting ourselves in all the disposals of his providence
holders: some, as reported by Matthew Henry

sides.position: Cease being the stranger a man has made himself, and keep up a constant correspondence
Treasure up, or procure an interest now with him

outliers.note: He alone reads the speech's two halves as a deliberate method, terrors from Mount Sinai followed by comforts from Mount Sion.

themes: sweet waters and bitter from one mouth
peace with God and with oneself
thereby good shall come unto thee
21.pericope_label: Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace

schools.summary: Gill denies that the law of Moses can be meant and takes the term for any doctrine or revelation handed down from the patriarchs.
Henry puts receiving in terms of government and insists the word must be retained as well as received.
Clarke insists with open impatience that the Mosaic Law is meant and calls the alternatives stuff and vanity; Wesley frames it as a choice of rule for the whole life.
Ellicott weighs the dating both ways and ends with the inner revelation of the voice of God in the conscience; Keil and Delitzsch render teaching and utterances rather than law and words.

debates.question: Does "the law" here mean the law of Moses?

sides.position: No; the term covers any doctrine or revelation made to the patriarchs and handed down
Yes, plainly, and the Noahic precepts and the law of nature are stuff and vanity
Probably not, since the life depicted is patriarchal, though "his words" is then hard to explain

outliers.note: He alone turns the dating difficulty into a positive suggestion, that the phrase witnesses to the inner revelation of the voice of God in the conscience.

themes: receive the law from his mouth
laying up the word in the heart
22.pericope_label: Receive the law from his mouth, and lay up his words

schools.summary: Gill reads encouragement in the all-sufficient name rather than demand, since the name signifies one who is sufficient to receive backsliders.
Henry presses the return home, quite to him, and finds three distinct assurances in the promise of gold.
Clarke takes being built up as a restored household and sets the versions of the gold clause side by side; Wesley makes the conditional emphatic and allows two senses of putting iniquity away.
Ellicott makes the gold clause a command to value treasure no more than brook stones; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the preposition and the verb for building up again.

debates.question: What is promised about the gold?

sides.position: Abundance greater than before, held by a surer tenure than iniquity got
That treasure be put on a level with the dust and valued no more than the stones of the brooks
The line is not fairly rendered at all, and the versions cannot be reconciled

outliers.note: He alone abandons the received rendering and lays rival versions side by side without choosing between them.

themes: a thorough return to the Almighty
23.pericope_label: If thou return to the Almighty, thou shalt be built up

schools.summary: Gill takes the defence in both registers, the gold already held and the soul kept as in a garrison, and makes the delight conditional on the affections being drawn off riches.
Henry contrasts what wealth usually does with the promised safety, and turns the delight round into the way of having one's heart's desire.
Clarke catalogues how the metals are got and then refuses the doctrine outright, setting the apostles against it; Wesley reduces the lifted face to looking up with cheerfulness.
Ellicott prefers treasure and precious silver and glosses the rare qualifier as brightness; Keil and Delitzsch render gold ore in abundance and silver of the brightest lustre.

debates.question: What is the Almighty promised to be?

sides.position: A defence, since the same word also signifies a strong-hold
A treasure, and precious silver

outliers.note: He alone rejects the theology of the promise, setting the apostolic doctrine of peace by faith and glorying in tribulation against the equation of prosperity with favour.

themes: prosperity as the mark of favour
25.pericope_label: The Almighty shall be thy defence, and thou shalt have delight

schools.summary: Gill draws the manner of prayer out of the verb, makes it privilege as well as duty, and offers three ways of taking a man's decree.
Henry turns the promise into an exchange of letters with heaven, and reads the established decree as inward satisfaction in outward affairs.
Clarke glosses the verb as unbosoming oneself and promises accomplishment of whatever is purposed in God's strength; Wesley lists the occasions of prayer and the ratifying of purposes.
Ellicott supplies Abraham's intercession for Sodom as the instance; Keil and Delitzsch render the decree as a devised plan that is then established.

debates.question: In what sense can a man decree a thing?

sides.position: Strictly only God can, since man appoints and God disappoints
As a magistrate, or in his own affairs, or best of all as a praying man
As grace framing his purposes so that the issue is to his heart's content

outliers.note: He alone sustains a figure of correspondence through the whole promise, letters sent by prayer, answered by providence, and replied to by praise.

27.pericope_label: Thou shalt make thy prayer unto him, and he shall hear thee

schools.summary: Gill takes the cast down for the wicked, and shows that the island cannot be an island, the word being a negative particle.
Henry describes the collapse and the lifting up, and reasons that the innocent need no deliverance, so that the promise must cover those who are not innocent.

Clarke calls the verse a great difficulty, offers a literal version with its Gospel parallel, and ends with a verdict on the whole speech; Wesley extends the deliverance to those who belong to the man addressed.
Ellicott calls the last word of Eliphaz a prophecy of how the book ends; Keil and Delitzsch suspect that the not-guiltless is Job himself in his present condition.

debates.question: Who is delivered in the last line?

sides.position: Every innocent person
The island or country, delivered by the innocent through their counsel and prayers
Him that is not innocent, delivered by the pureness of another man's hands

outliers.note: He alone closes with a verdict on the speech as a whole, which began with the bitterest charges and ended with common-place exhortations, yielding scarcely one important maxim.

29.pericope_label: He shall save the humble person, and deliver the island of the innocent
